title: An entangling Hubbard quasiparticle collider on a digital quantum processor
authors: Chan Bin Bark, Hanbyul Kim, Yoonil Koo, SeungBeom Hong, Seik Pak, Kwang Jun Ahn, Sangmo Cheon, Youngseok Kim, Moon Jip Park
abstract: Scattering of quasiparticles provides direct access to the interactions that govern strongly correlated systems. In this work, we realize the quasiparticle scattering experiment of the Fermi-Hubbard model on a digital quantum processor by colliding a doublon and a holon in the half-filled chain of 21 sites encoded on 42 qubits of the ibm_boston processor. For the first time, we measure the transmission probability of quasiparticles of the Hubbard model on quantum hardware, which agrees with the Bethe-ansatz scattering matrix without free parameters. Beyond the scattering probabilities, the collision generates entanglement by superposing the transmitted and reflected components, which we infer from the particle-number fluctuation. In sharp contrast, a control collision between two doublons shows neither the interaction dependence nor the number fluctuation, as expected for indistinguishable particles. Our work demonstrates that the ability to create quasiparticles of a chosen flavor on demand and program their motion and interactions makes a digital quantum processor a new experimental toolset for probing the entanglement structure generated by quasiparticle scattering.
summary: This work demonstrates the first measurement of quasiparticle scattering in the Fermi-Hubbard model on a quantum processor by colliding doublons and holons. The results confirm theoretical predictions for the scattering matrix and quantify the entanglement generated during the collision. This establishes the quantum processor as a powerful new tool for probing strongly correlated electron physics.
main_problem: To experimentally realize and measure quasiparticle scattering (doublon-holon collision) in the Fermi-Hubbard model on a digital quantum processor to probe interaction-driven physics.
main_result: The measured transmission probability agrees with the Bethe-ansatz scattering matrix, and the collision generates measurable entanglement, which is absent in control collisions between identical quasiparticles.
method: The study combines quantum simulation on a superconducting quantum processor with advanced error mitigation techniques (symmetry restoration) and theoretical analysis using scattering theory.
model_or_system: The Fermi-Hubbard model is simulated on a half-filled 1D chain using a digital quantum processor (IBM superconducting qubits). Quasiparticles (doublons and holons) are created and their collision dynamics are measured.
key_observables: Transmission probability ($T$), entanglement entropy ($S_{	ext{num}}$), particle-number fluctuation ($	ext{Var}(N_L)$), and charge density maps.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$) relative to hopping ($J$), and the system size ($L=21$ sites).
main_assumptions: The collision is assumed to be elastic, and the measurement of entanglement relies on inferring coherence from particle-number fluctuations rather than full state tomography.
figures_summary: Figures show space-time maps of charge density during propagation and collision for varying $U/J$. Key plots quantify $T$ vs. $U$, and compare particle number variance for different collision types (d-h vs. d-d).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from setting up the quasiparticle scattering experiment on the quantum hardware, measuring the transmission probability $T$ and comparing it to theory, to quantifying the generated entanglement via particle number fluctuations, and finally detailing the necessary error mitigation techniques.
why_interesting: It bridges the gap between highly complex, strongly correlated theoretical models (like the Hubbard model) and near-term quantum hardware capabilities, providing a concrete, measurable testbed for many-body physics.
